title: Chapter 10 — Security and Privacy: Quality Question Bank

questions.question: What is the book's "power of negative thinking" principle, and why does it recommend applying it to security?
options: Actively considering worst-case/disaster scenarios lets you prepare for and prevent them — citing the argument that positive thinking can blind people to real risks
It means always assuming a project will fail, so no effort should be invested in it
It's a way to deliberately lower stakeholder expectations for a project
It refers to reducing energy costs in low-power data centers
questions.explanation: The book cites Atul Gawande's argument that "positive thinking can blind us to the possibility of terrorist attacks or medical emergencies and deter preparation. Negative thinking allows us to consider disastrous scenarios and act to prevent them."

questions.question: What's the best way to protect private/sensitive data, according to the book's "power of negative thinking" discussion?
options: Avoid ingesting or collecting sensitive data in the first place unless there's an actual downstream need for it
Always encrypt every dataset twice, regardless of its actual sensitivity or use case
Store all sensitive data in a single, extremely well-guarded central vault
Immediately anonymize all data upon collection, with no other precaution needed
questions.explanation: The book states: "Data engineers should actively think through the scenarios for data utilization and collect sensitive data only if there is an actual need downstream. The best way to protect private and sensitive data is to avoid ingesting this data in the first place."

questions.question: What's the difference between "security theater" and genuine security habit, as the book describes them?
options: Security theater is compliance-driven box-checking (unread policies, forgotten annual reviews) that creates an illusion of security; genuine habitual security is baked into culture through regular, simple, real practice
Security theater refers only to physical office security and has nothing to do with data
Genuine security habit means having zero written security policies at all
Security theater and genuine security habit are the same thing described two ways
questions.explanation: The book contrasts "security policies in the hundreds of pages that nobody reads" (security theater, "done in the letter of compliance... without real commitment") with pursuing "genuine and habitual security" baked into culture.

questions.question: What does "active security" mean, per the book, as opposed to a standard compliance checklist approach?
options: Actively researching real threats and thinking through your organization's specific vulnerabilities, rather than passively following a generic checklist
Hiring only external security auditors and taking no further internal action
It refers exclusively to automated intrusion detection software
It means disabling all employee access until a breach is actually detected
questions.explanation: The book contrasts "simply deploying scheduled simulated phishing attacks" or "a standard compliance checklist" with actively "researching successful phishing attacks and thinking through your organizational security vulnerabilities."

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model in the cloud, who does the book say is generally responsible for most cloud security breaches?
options: The customer/end user — most breaches happen due to misconfigurations, mistakes, and oversights on the customer's side, not the cloud provider's infrastructure
The cloud vendor is described as responsible for every breach, regardless of configuration
Responsibility is randomly assigned by the vendor's legal team after each incident
Breaches are described as evenly split 50/50 with no discernible pattern
questions.explanation: The book states: "Most cloud security breaches continue to be caused by end users, not the cloud. Breaches occur because of unintended misconfigurations, mistakes, oversights, and sloppiness."

questions.question: The book recommends putting rarely-needed sensitive data behind a "broken glass" process. What does this mean, and when is access revoked?
options: Users can access the data only after an emergency approval process; access is revoked immediately once the work is done
"Broken glass" means the data is permanently deleted the first time it's accessed
It means giving every employee standing access to the data, just in case of emergency
It refers to encrypting data with a key that automatically changes on every access
questions.explanation: The book describes it exactly this way: "users can access it only after going through an emergency approval process to fix a problem... Access is revoked immediately once the work is done."

questions.question: What are the book's basic credential-handling rules for individuals?
options: Use SSO with multifactor authentication by default, never share passwords, disable/delete old credentials, never put credentials in code (use a secrets manager), and apply least privilege
Rotate every password weekly regardless of whether SSO is in use
Store shared credentials in a team spreadsheet for convenience
Credentials should be embedded in code comments so teammates can find them easily
questions.explanation: The book's example security policy lists exactly these rules: SSO-first with MFA, never sharing credentials, deleting old ones, never committing secrets to code, and always applying least privilege.

questions.question: Why does the book say HTTPS alone doesn't fully protect data, using the example of public S3 buckets?
options: HTTPS encrypts data in transit, but does nothing to prevent a leak if the storage itself has been left with open/public permissions — a separate access-control failure
HTTPS is described as fully obsolete and should never be used at all
HTTPS actually makes public bucket permissions less risky, according to the book
The book states S3 buckets cannot be encrypted under any circumstances
questions.explanation: The book states: "HTTPS does nothing to protect data if bucket permissions are left open to the public, another cause of several data scandals over the last decade."

questions.question: What four areas does the book recommend actively monitoring for security purposes?
options: Access (who's accessing what and from where), resource usage (disk/CPU/memory/I/O anomalies), billing (unexpected spending spikes), and excess/unused permissions
Only network bandwidth, with nothing else needing regular monitoring
Only employee badge-swipe logs for the physical office
Exclusively the hardware age of each employee's laptop
questions.explanation: The book lists exactly these four monitoring areas: access, resources, billing, and excess permissions, recommending they be combined into a single cross-sectional view.

questions.question: Why does the book argue the cloud is generally a more secure default than an on-premises hardened perimeter for most organizations?
options: The cloud is closer to a zero-trust model (every action requires authentication) and lets organizations leverage the security engineering resources of major cloud providers
On-premises servers are described as incapable of encryption under any configuration
Cloud providers are described as guaranteeing zero breaches will ever occur
Air-gapped servers are described as inherently and always insecure
questions.explanation: The book states: "The cloud is generally closer to zero-trust security—every action requires authentication. We believe that the cloud is a more secure option for most organizations because... [it] allows companies to leverage the army of security engineers employed by the public clouds."

questions.question: What does the book say about where security should rank in a data engineer's job?
options: Security is the first thing a data engineer needs to think about in every aspect of their job and every stage of the lifecycle, since one security breach or data leak can leave a business dead in the water
Security is an afterthought to be handled only when time permits
Security only matters at the serving stage
Security is solely the job of dedicated security teams
questions.explanation: The book says security is the first thing to consider in every aspect of the job, since a breach can be devastating.

questions.question: Why does the book say privacy is a key ingredient for trust, and what private data do engineers handle?
options: Privacy has long been critical to trust, and engineers directly or indirectly handle financial information, private communications, medical history, educational records, and job history
Privacy only matters for external customers
Engineers never touch private data
Privacy and trust are unrelated
questions.explanation: The book lists the types of private data engineers handle and privacy's role in trust.

questions.question: What privacy laws does the book cite as examples, and what does it say about their penalties?
options: FERPA in the 1970s, HIPAA in the 1990s, and GDPR in the mid-2010s — penalties for violation can be significant, even devastating, to a business
Only GDPR, which has no penalties
No privacy laws exist
HIPAA applies only to retail
questions.explanation: The book cites FERPA, HIPAA, and GDPR and warns of significant penalties.

questions.question: How do a data engineer's security responsibilities vary between organizations?
options: At a small startup a data engineer may do double duty as a data security engineer, while at a large tech company armies of security engineers exist — but data engineers can still identify and mitigate vulnerabilities within their own teams and systems
Responsibilities are identical at every organization
Data engineers never have security duties
Only security engineers handle security
questions.explanation: The book describes how responsibilities vary and that engineers can still identify vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Who does the book call the weakest link in security and privacy, and what posture does it recommend?
options: You — security is often compromised at the human level, so conduct yourself as if you're always a target, take a defensive posture, and be paranoid
The cloud provider
The antivirus software
External hackers only
questions.explanation: The book says the weakest link is you and recommends a defensive, paranoid posture.

questions.question: What does the book recommend when someone asks you for your credentials?
options: Hold off and get second opinions from coworkers and friends, confirming the request is legitimate — a quick chat or phone call is cheaper than a ransomware attack triggered through an email click
Always comply immediately
Email the credentials as requested
Ignore all requests without verification
questions.explanation: The book recommends extreme doubt and verification before sharing credentials.

questions.question: Who should you trust at face value when asked for credentials or sensitive information, per the book?
options: Trust nobody — including your coworkers — when asked for credentials, sensitive data, or confidential information
Trust all coworkers always
Trust anyone who looks official
Trust only people you've met once
questions.explanation: The book says to trust nobody at face value, including coworkers.

questions.question: How does the book describe a data engineer's role as the first line of defense in privacy and ethics?
options: If you're uncomfortable with sensitive data you've been tasked to collect or have ethical questions, raise concerns with colleagues and leadership and ensure your work is both legally compliant and ethical
Ethical concerns should be kept private
Compliance is the only concern
Data engineers have no ethical responsibilities
questions.explanation: The book says engineers are the first line of defense and should raise ethical concerns.

questions.question: What does the book say happens when people follow regular security processes?
options: Security becomes part of the job — make it a habit, regularly practice real security, exercise the principle of least privilege, and understand the shared responsibility model in the cloud
Security becomes an afterthought
Regular practice weakens security
Habits are irrelevant to security
questions.explanation: The book says regular security processes make security part of the job.

questions.question: What problem does the book describe with a pervasive focus on compliance rather than bad scenarios?
options: It creates an illusion of security but often leaves gaping holes that would be evident with a few minutes of reflection
Compliance always eliminates all risks
Bad scenarios are impossible to predict
Compliance focus never has downsides
questions.explanation: The book says compliance focus creates an illusion of security with gaping holes.

questions.question: How does the book say security needs to be for it to become habitual, and what practice does it cite from its own company?
options: Security needs to be simple and effective enough to become habitual; the authors' company runs security training and policy review at least once a month to ingrain it into the team's DNA
Security must be complex to be effective
Annual reviews are sufficient
Training more than once a year is wasteful
questions.explanation: The book recommends simple, effective, habitual security with monthly training/review.

questions.question: Who does the book say is responsible for security?
options: Everyone — each person is responsible and has a role to play; it must be the priority for you and everyone else you work with
Only the CISO
Only security engineers
Nobody is responsible
questions.explanation: The book says everyone is responsible and security must be the priority.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege, and what antipattern does the book describe?
options: A person or system should be given only the privileges and data needed to complete the task at hand and nothing more; the antipattern is giving a regular user carte blanche administrative access when they need just a handful of IAM roles
Everyone should have maximum privileges
Least privilege means no access at all
Administrative access for all is recommended
questions.explanation: The book defines least privilege and warns against giving carte blanche admin access.

questions.question: How should IAM roles be granted and revoked, and what does the book say about service accounts?
options: Provide the user (or their group) the IAM roles they need when they need them and take them away when no longer needed; treat humans and machines (service accounts) the same way
Grant all roles permanently
Service accounts need unlimited privileges
Roles should never be revoked
questions.explanation: The book says to grant roles as needed and revoke them, treating humans and service accounts equally.

questions.question: How does least privilege support privacy, and what access-control techniques does the book recommend?
options: Users expect people to look at sensitive data only when necessary; implement column, row, and cell-level access controls, consider masking PII, and create views containing only the information the viewer needs
Privacy is not related to access control
Only column-level controls are needed
Masking PII is never recommended
questions.explanation: The book ties least privilege to privacy and recommends column/row/cell controls, masking, and views.

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, what is the cloud vendor responsible for versus the customer?
options: The vendor is responsible for the physical security of its data center and hardware; the customer is responsible for the security of the applications and systems they build and maintain in the cloud
The vendor is responsible for everything
The customer is responsible for the data center's physical security
Neither party has responsibilities
questions.explanation: The book splits responsibility: vendor for physical data center/hardware security, customer for their applications and systems.

questions.question: Why does the book say you need to back up your data regularly, and what should you test?
options: Data disappears — dead drives, accidental deletions, or bad actors locking data away in ransomware attacks — so back up regularly for disaster recovery and business continuity, and test the restoration of your backups on a regular basis
Data never disappears
Backups are unnecessary
Restoration testing is wasteful
questions.explanation: The book recommends regular backups for disaster recovery and testing restorations.

questions.question: Under what larger heading does the book place data backup, and why is it adjacent to security?
options: Data backup goes under the larger heading of disaster prevention, but it's adjacent to security, especially in the era of ransomware attacks
It is purely a security practice
It is unrelated to security
It belongs under billing
questions.explanation: The book places backup under disaster prevention, adjacent to security.

questions.question: What does the book say about the format of its sample security policy?
options: They don't overcomplicate things — they give people a short list of practical actions they can take immediately
It is hundreds of pages long
It requires annual reviews nobody reads
It is too complex to follow
questions.explanation: The book says the sample policy is a short list of practical, immediate actions.

questions.question: What does the book recommend about single sign-on (SSO) and passwords?
options: Use SSO for everything, avoid passwords whenever possible, and use SSO as the default
Use passwords instead of SSO
SSO should be avoided
Passwords are the preferred default
questions.explanation: The book recommends SSO for everything as the default.

questions.question: What does the book recommend about sharing passwords and credentials?
options: Don't share passwords or credentials, including client passwords and credentials; if in doubt, see the person you report to, and keep digging until you find an answer
Sharing credentials is fine among teammates
Client passwords can be shared freely
Doubts should be ignored
questions.explanation: The book says never to share passwords or credentials and to seek answers when in doubt.

questions.question: What does the book say about old credentials and credentials in code?
options: Disable or delete old credentials (preferably delete), and never put credentials in code — handle secrets as configuration, never commit them to version control, and use a secrets manager where possible
Keep old credentials active forever
Embed credentials in code for convenience
Commit secrets to version control
questions.explanation: The book recommends deleting old credentials and using secrets managers instead of code-embedded credentials.

questions.question: What does the book recommend about device management?
options: Use device management for all employee devices so they can be remotely wiped if an employee leaves or a device is lost, use MFA for all devices, and sign in with company email credentials
Devices need no management
Lost devices are not a concern
MFA is only for cloud accounts
questions.explanation: The book recommends device management with remote wipe, MFA, and company email sign-in.

questions.question: What does the book say about treating your device and screen sharing?
options: Treat your device as an extension of yourself and don't let it out of your sight; when screen sharing, share only single documents, browser tabs, or windows, avoid sharing your full desktop, and share only what's required
Devices can be left unattended
Full desktop sharing is always fine
Screen sharing details don't matter
questions.explanation: The book recommends guarding devices and sharing only what's needed on screens.

questions.question: What video-call and software-update habits does the book recommend?
options: Use do-not-disturb mode on video calls so messages don't appear during calls or recordings; restart your browser on update alerts, run minor OS updates, follow company guidance on critical major OS updates, don't use beta OS versions, and wait a week or two for new major OS releases
Messages should appear during calls
Ignore all update alerts
Use beta OS versions immediately
questions.explanation: The book lists these video-call and update habits.

questions.question: Why should you always patch and update operating systems and software?
options: Software gets stale and vulnerabilities are constantly discovered, so patching avoids exposing a security flaw in an older version of the tools you're using
Updates always introduce vulnerabilities
Stale software is more secure
Vulnerabilities are never discovered
questions.explanation: The book says patching avoids exposing flaws in older software versions.

questions.question: How can engineers keep their own code and dependencies updated?
options: Automate builds or set alerts on releases and vulnerabilities so you can be prompted to perform the updates manually, since many SaaS and cloud-managed services already automate upgrades
Updates only happen automatically everywhere
Manual updates are never needed
Dependencies never become vulnerable
questions.explanation: The book recommends automating builds or setting release/vulnerability alerts.

questions.question: What does the book say encryption will and won't do?
options: Encryption is not a magic bullet — it will do little against a human security breach that grants credentials, but it's a baseline requirement that protects from basic attacks like network traffic interception
Encryption protects against all human breaches
Encryption is optional
Encryption only protects against physical theft
questions.explanation: The book says encryption is a baseline that won't help against credential-granting human breaches.

questions.question: What encryption-at-rest measures does the book recommend?
options: Full-disk encryption on company laptops, server-side encryption for servers/filesystems/databases/object storage, encrypted backups, and application-level encryption where applicable
Only encrypt databases
Encryption at rest is optional
Only encrypt backups
questions.explanation: The book lists these encryption-at-rest measures.

questions.question: Why should data engineers always be aware of how keys are handled?
options: Bad key handling is a significant source of data leaks
Keys are irrelevant to security
Key handling never causes leaks
Only the cloud provider handles keys
questions.explanation: The book calls bad key handling a significant source of data leaks.

questions.question: What does the book say about FTP and other older protocols?
options: FTP is simply not secure on a public network and is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks where an attacker intercepts and changes downloaded data — it's best to avoid FTP
FTP is fully secure
Man-in-the-middle attacks are impossible
FTP is recommended on public networks
questions.explanation: The book warns against FTP due to man-in-the-middle vulnerability.

questions.question: What general advice does the book give about encryption over the wire?
options: Make sure everything is encrypted over the wire, even with legacy protocols; when in doubt, use robust technology with encryption baked in
Encryption over the wire is optional
Legacy protocols need no encryption
Only new protocols encrypt
questions.explanation: The book advises encrypting everything over the wire including legacy protocols.

questions.question: Why is automated monitoring, logging, and alerting important for security?
options: Hackers don't announce they're infiltrating your systems and most companies find out well after the fact, so set up automated monitoring, logging, and alerting to be aware of peculiar events, with automatic anomaly detection if possible
Companies always detect breaches instantly
Monitoring is unnecessary
Hackers always announce intrusions
questions.explanation: The book recommends automated monitoring/logging/alerting because breaches are detected late.

questions.question: What should access monitoring look for, according to the book?
options: Who's accessing what, when, and from where; new accesses granted; strange patterns like users accessing systems they usually don't or shouldn't; and new unrecognized users — comb through access logs, users, and roles regularly
Only login counts
Only failed password attempts
Access logs need no review
questions.explanation: The book describes the access-monitoring areas to review.

questions.question: Why should billing be monitored for security?
options: An unexpected spike in billing might indicate someone or something is utilizing your resources for malicious purposes; set up budget alerts to make sure spending is within expectations
Billing has no security relevance
Spending spikes are always innocent
Budget alerts are unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book links unexpected billing spikes to possible malicious resource use.

questions.question: How do vendors' excess-permission monitoring tools work, and what example does the book give?
options: They monitor for permissions not utilized by a user or service account over time and can alert an administrator or remove permissions after an elapsed time — e.g. removing an analyst's Redshift permissions after six months of no access
They grant more permissions automatically
Unused permissions are never removed
Redshift access never expires
questions.explanation: The book describes unused-permission monitoring with the six-month Redshift example.

questions.question: How does the book recommend combining the four monitoring areas?
options: Combine them into a single cross-sectional view of resource, access, and billing profile, set up a dashboard for everyone on the data team, and couple it with an incident response plan run through regularly
Monitor each area in isolation
Only executives see monitoring
Incident response plans need no practice
questions.explanation: The book recommends a combined cross-sectional dashboard and rehearsed incident response.

questions.question: What examples of terrible network security practices does the book give?
options: Publicly available S3 buckets housing sensitive data, EC2 instances with inbound SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0, and databases with open access to all inbound requests over the public internet
Properly firewalled databases
Whitelisted SSH access
Encrypted storage buckets
questions.explanation: The book cites these open-access examples as terrible network security.

questions.question: What network-access basics should a data engineer be aware of even if network security is left to experts?
options: Understand what IPs and ports are open, to whom, and why; whitelist the incoming IP addresses of systems and users that will access these ports; and avoid broadly opening connections for any reason
Open all ports to the world
Never whitelist IPs
Port access details don't matter
questions.explanation: The book recommends understanding open IPs/ports and whitelisting.

questions.question: What does the book advise about accessing the cloud or SaaS tools?
options: Use an encrypted connection — don't use an unencrypted website from a coffee shop
Public Wi-Fi is always safe
Encryption is optional for SaaS
Coffee shop Wi-Fi needs no caution
questions.explanation: The book advises encrypted connections, including avoiding unencrypted sites on public Wi-Fi.

questions.question: What does the book say about air-gapped servers?
options: They are the ultimate example of a hardened security perimeter (nuclear missile silos are air gapped), but even on premises they remain vulnerable to human security failings
Air-gapped servers are invulnerable
Air gapping is a cloud concept
Human failings can't affect air-gapped servers
questions.explanation: The book describes air-gapped servers as the ultimate hardened perimeter yet still human-vulnerable.

questions.question: What does the book say about security at the level of low-level data engineering components?
options: Every software library, storage system, or compute node is a potential security vulnerability — a flaw in an obscure logging library might bypass access controls, and even CPU architectures and microcode are potential vulnerabilities, so no link in the chain can be taken for granted
Only application code has vulnerabilities
Hardware can never be compromised
Libraries are always secure
questions.explanation: The book says every element is a potential vulnerability, from libraries to CPU microcode.

questions.question: Why should every technology employee think about security problems in their domain of expertise?
options: Every technology contributor develops a domain of expertise, and experts in a particular technology are well positioned to identify security holes in it — even if the company employs security researchers
Only security researchers can find holes
Domain expertise is irrelevant to security
Engineers should leave security to others
questions.explanation: The book says domain experts are well positioned to identify security holes.

questions.question: What role should data engineers take when they identify potential security risks in their systems?
options: Think through mitigations and take an active role in deploying them
Report and do nothing further
Wait for someone else to act
Ignore the risk
questions.explanation: The book says engineers should think through mitigations and deploy them.

questions.question: How does the book conclude its security advice for data engineers?
options: Security needs to be a habit of mind and action; treat data like your wallet or smartphone, and although you may not be in charge of security, knowing basic practices and keeping security top of mind helps reduce the risk of breaches
Only security teams need security habits
Data can be treated carelessly
Basic practices are unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book concludes with security as a habit of mind and action.
